` (the recipe name), and it must come before any `

`. - At least **two** `

` headings ("Ingredients" and "Method"). - The ingredients are an **unordered list** with at least three items. - The method is an **ordered list** with exactly four steps (do not type the numbers yourself). - No `
` elements and no `` elements remain.

web-links-images.title: Links and images with alt text
web-links-images.description:
Finish the markup of a small walking-club page. Requirements: - A `
` containing exactly **three** links, each with an `href`. - One of the nav links jumps within the page: its `href` is `#contact`, and an element with `id="contact"` exists. - An **external** link whose `href` starts with `https://` opens in a new tab (`target="_blank"`) and has `rel="noopener"`. - The photo (``) has meaningful `alt` text of at least five characters, plus `width` and `height` attributes. - The decorative divider (``) has an **empty** `alt` attribute (present, but `""`).
web-links-images.starter:
Home Walks

Hill Walkers

We follow the route notes published by the national trail office.

Contact

Email the secretary to join a walk.
web-links-images.solution:
Home Walks Contact

Hill Walkers

We follow the route notes published by the national trail office (opens in a new tab).

Contact

Email the secretary to join a walk.

checks.name: The nav holds exactly three links with href
A link points to #contact and that id exists
The external link opens in a new tab with rel=noopener
The photo has descriptive alt text
The photo has width and height attributes
The divider has an empty alt attribute

guide.prereqs: The `` element, relative and fragment URLs, `` and its `alt`, `width` and `height` attributes. See *Lists and links* and *Images*.
guide.intuition: A link without `href` is not a link: it cannot be focused or followed. An image without `alt` is a mystery to anyone who cannot see it. Decorative images still need the attribute, set to an empty string, to say "skip me".
hints: Give every `<a>` in the nav an `href`, and add the missing third link.
A fragment link has the form `href="#some-id"`; the target needs the matching `id`. The Contact heading is a natural target.
For the external link add both `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener"`. For the divider write `alt=""`, which is different from leaving `alt` out.
guide.approach: 1. Add `href` values to Home and Walks and a third link `Contact`. 2. Put `id="contact"` on the Contact heading. 3. Add `target="_blank" rel="noopener"` to the https link and say in its text that it opens a new tab. 4. Describe the photo in `alt` and state its intrinsic size with `width="320" height="180"`. 5. Add `alt=""` to the divider.
guide.pitfalls:
- `alt="image"` or `alt="photo"` describes nothing.
- Omitting `alt` on the divider makes some screen readers read the file name.
- Forgetting the `#` in the fragment link, which would request a file called `contact`.

web-figure-caption.title: Figure with a caption
web-figure-caption.description:
A chart is followed by a loose paragraph acting as its caption. Tie them together properly.

Requirements:

- The image is inside a `<figure>` element, together with a `<figcaption>` holding the caption text.
- The `<figcaption>` is a direct child of the `<figure>`.
- The image keeps a non-empty `alt` that is **not identical** to the caption text.
- The figure has **no outer margin** (browsers add 40px at the sides by default).
- The image never overflows its container: its computed `max-width` is `100%`.
web-figure-caption.starter:
Rainfall report

Figure 1. The hills were wettest in the west.

The eastern slopes stayed dry for most of the month.
web-figure-caption.solution:
Rainfall report

The eastern slopes stayed dry for most of the month.

checks.name: The image is inside a figure
The figure has a figcaption child with text
The image has non-empty alt text
The alt text differs from the caption
The figure has no side margins
The image has max-width: 100%

guide.prereqs: `<figure>`, `<figcaption>`, alt text and fluid images. See *Images*.
guide.intuition: A paragraph placed under a picture is a caption only to the eye. `<figure>` groups an illustration with its `<figcaption>` so that software knows they belong together. The caption adds context for everyone; the `alt` replaces the picture for people who cannot see it. They do different jobs, so they should not repeat each other.
hints: Wrap the `` and the caption sentence in one `

Change the caption's `

` to `
Reset the browser default with `figure { margin: 0; }` and make the image fluid with `max-width: 100%; height: auto;`.
guide.approach:
1. Add `<figure>` around the image and caption.
2. Replace the caption paragraph with `<figcaption>`.
3. Write `alt` text that says what the picture shows, in words different from the caption.
4. In the CSS, remove the figure's margin and give the image `max-width: 100%` and `height: auto`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Copying the caption into `alt`, so a screen reader hears it twice.
- Putting the `<figcaption>` outside the `<figure>`.
- Forgetting that `figure` has a default 40px side margin.

web-data-table.title: Accessible data table
web-data-table.description:
The opening hours below are marked up with only `<tr>` and `<td>`. Turn them into an accessible data table.

Requirements:

- The table has a `<caption>` (first child of the table) with text.
- A `<thead>` contains one row of **three** column headers: `<th scope="col">`.
- A `<tbody>` contains **three** rows; the first cell of each is a row header `<th scope="row">`, followed by two `<td>` cells (six `<td>` in total in the body).
- A `<tfoot>` contains exactly one row.
- Borders are collapsed: the table's computed `border-collapse` is `collapse`.
web-data-table.starter:
Library opening hours

DayOpensCloses
Weekdays09:0019:00
Saturday10:0016:00
SundayClosedClosed
Bank holidaysSee the notice board
web-data-table.solution:
Library opening hours
DayOpensCloses
Weekdays09:0019:00
Saturday10:0016:00
SundayClosedClosed
Bank holidaysSee the notice board

checks.name: The table starts with a caption that has text
thead has three th with scope=col
tbody has three rows
Each body row starts with th scope=row
The body has six td data cells
tfoot has exactly one row
Borders are collapsed

guide.prereqs: `caption`, `thead`, `tbody`, `tfoot`, `th` and the `scope` attribute; `border-collapse`. See *Tables for tabular data*.
guide.intuition: A data cell such as "19:00" only means something with its two labels: the row ("Weekdays") and the column ("Closes"). Marking labels as `<th>` with a `scope` lets a screen reader announce them as the user moves through the grid. The caption names the whole table.
hints: Move the bold paragraph's text into a `<caption>` placed immediately after `<table>`.
The first row holds column labels: wrap it in `<thead>` and change its cells to `<th scope="col">`. In the other rows only the first cell is a label: `<th scope="row">`.
Wrap the three day rows in `<tbody>` and the bank-holiday row in `<tfoot>`. Add `table { border-collapse: collapse; }` and extend the border rule to `th` as well as `td`.
guide.approach:
1. Replace the paragraph with `<caption>Library opening hours</caption>` inside the table.
2. Create `<thead>` with the header row and three `th scope="col"`.
3. Create `<tbody>` with the Weekdays, Saturday and Sunday rows, each starting with `th scope="row"`.
4. Create `<tfoot>` with the bank-holiday row.
5. Style: `border-collapse: collapse` on the table and borders/padding on `th, td`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Leaving the heading as a separate paragraph: it is not connected to the table.
- Using `scope="col"` on the row headers.
- Putting the bank-holiday row in `tbody`, which makes four body rows.
- Styling only `td`, so the new `th` cells lose their borders.

web-aspect-ratio-box.title: A 16:9 media box
web-aspect-ratio-box.description: A video thumbnail must keep a widescreen shape at every width, and its picture must fill the box without being stretched. Write the CSS for `.media` and for the image inside it. Requirements: - `.media` is as wide as its container but never wider than **640px**. - `.media` has an `aspect-ratio` of **16 / 9** (so its height follows its width). - The `` fills the box exactly (same width and height as `.media`). - The image uses `object-fit: cover`, so it is cropped instead of distorted. - Do not set a fixed `height` in pixels on `.media`.
web-aspect-ratio-box.starter: Episode 4: crossing the ridge
web-aspect-ratio-box.solution: Episode 4: crossing the ridge

checks.name: .media is 640px wide in this 1024px frame
.media has aspect-ratio 16 / 9
The box is rendered in a 16:9 shape
The image fills the box exactly
checks.test: ((b, i) => Math.abs(b.width - i.width) < 1 && Math.abs(b.height - i.height) < 1)(document.querySelector('.media').getBoundingClientRect(), document.querySelector('.media img').getBoundingClientRect())

checks.name: The image uses object-fit: cover

guide.prereqs: `max-width`, `aspect-ratio` and `object-fit`. See *Backgrounds, gradients and sizing images with CSS*.
guide.intuition: `aspect-ratio` lets a box derive its height from its width, so the shape survives any resize. The picture inside is square, so forcing it into a 16:9 box would squash it. `object-fit: cover` scales it until the box is covered and crops the overflow.
hints: Give `.media` `width: 100%` and cap it with `max-width: 640px`.
Add `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;` and do not write any `height` on `.media`.
Make the image take the whole box with `width: 100%; height: 100%;` and choose the cropping behaviour with `object-fit: cover`. `display: block` removes the inline gap under the image.
guide.approach:
1. `.media { width: 100%; max-width: 640px; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }`
2. `.media img { display: block; width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover; }`
3. Check: at 640px wide the box is 360px tall, and the square picture is cropped top and bottom.
guide.pitfalls:
- Setting `height: 360px`: the shape breaks as soon as the width changes.
- Forgetting `height: 100%` on the image, so it keeps its own square shape and overflows the box.
- Leaving the default `object-fit: fill`, which stretches the picture.

web-accessible-form.title: An accessible sign-up form
web-accessible-form.description:
The sign-up form below shows text next to its controls, but nothing is connected. Repair it.

Requirements:

- The `<form>` submits with the **post** method.
- Every visible control (`input`, `select`, `textarea`) has a programmatically associated `<label>` (wrap it, or use `for` + `id`), and every control has a `name`.
- The control with `id="name"` is required.
- The control with `id="email"` has `type="email"` and is required.
- The three membership options are radio buttons that share **one** `name`, grouped in a `<fieldset>` that has a `<legend>`.
- The form has a submit button.
web-accessible-form.starter:
Full name
Email
Membership Solo Family Student
Branch
Anything we should know?
Join
web-accessible-form.solution: Membership

checks.name: The form uses method post
Every control has an associated label
checks.test: (c => c.length >= 7 && c.every(e => e.labels && e.labels.length > 0))([...document.querySelectorAll('form input, form select, form textarea')])

checks.name: Every control has a name
checks.test: [...document.querySelectorAll('form input, form select, form textarea')].every(e => e.name.length > 0)

checks.name: #name is required
#email is type=email and required
The three radios share one name inside a fieldset with a legend
There is a real submit button

guide.prereqs: `form`, `label`, `name`, input types, radio groups, `fieldset`/`legend`, `required`. See *Forms: collecting input*.
guide.intuition: Text beside a field is not a label until the two are linked. The link is what makes a screen reader announce "Email, edit text" and what makes a click on the words focus the field. Radio buttons exclude one another only when they share a `name`, and a group of them needs a `legend` to say what question they answer.
hints: For the text fields, wrap the visible words in `<label for="...">` using the control's existing `id`.
Give all three radios the same `name`, wrap each one in its own `<label>`, and wrap the whole group in `<fieldset>` with `<legend>Membership</legend>`.
Add `name` to every control, `required` where asked, change the email field's `type`, set `method="post"` on the form, and replace the clickable `div` with `<button type="submit">`.
guide.approach:
1. `<form action="/join" method="post">`.
2. Name field: `<label for="name">` + `name="name" required`.
3. Email field: `type="email" name="email" required` with a label.
4. Radios: one shared `name`, each wrapped in a label, inside `fieldset` + `legend`.
5. Select and textarea: labels and names.
6. Replace the `div onclick` with a real submit button.
guide.pitfalls:
- A `placeholder` is not a label.
- A `for` value that does not exactly match an `id` connects nothing.
- Different radio names allow all three to be selected at once.
- A `div` with a click handler cannot be reached by keyboard and does not submit on Enter.

web-form-validation.title: Validation attributes
web-form-validation.description:
Add built-in validation to the registration form using **HTML attributes only** (no JavaScript).

Requirements:

- `#username`: required, between **3** and **12** characters, and only lowercase letters and digits are valid (use `pattern`).
- `#age`: a number input, required, minimum **18**, maximum **99**.
- `#website`: a URL input that is **optional**.
- `#password`: a password input, required, at least **8** characters.
- `#terms`: a checkbox that must be ticked.
- The form must **not** have the `novalidate` attribute.
web-form-validation.starter:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Register</title>
<style>
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
form { display: grid; gap: .7rem; max-width: 22rem; }
label { display: grid; gap: .2rem; }
input, button { font: inherit; }
input:user-invalid { border: 2px solid #c62828; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/register" method="post" novalidate>
  <label>Username <input id="username" name="username"></label>
  <label>Age <input id="age" name="age"></label>
  <label>Website (optional) <input id="website" name="website"></label>
  <label>Password <input id="password" name="password"></label>
  <label style="display:block"><input id="terms" name="terms" type="checkbox"> I accept the terms</label>
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>
web-form-validation.solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Register</title>
<style>
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
form { display: grid; gap: .7rem; max-width: 22rem; }
label { display: grid; gap: .2rem; }
input, button { font: inherit; }
input:user-invalid { border: 2px solid #c62828; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<form action="/register" method="post">
  <label>Username <input id="username" name="username" required minlength="3" maxlength="12" pattern="[a-z0-9]+" autocomplete="username"></label>
  <label>Age <input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="18" max="99" required></label>
  <label>Website (optional) <input id="website" name="website" type="url"></label>
  <label>Password <input id="password" name="password" type="password" required minlength="8" autocomplete="new-password"></label>
  <label style="display:block"><input id="terms" name="terms" type="checkbox" required> I accept the terms</label>
  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>

checks.name: Username is required with length 3 to 12
Username pattern rejects 'Bad Name' and accepts 'walker42'
checks.test: (u => { u.value = 'Bad Name'; const bad = u.validity.patternMismatch; u.value = 'walker42'; const good = !u.validity.patternMismatch; u.value = ''; return bad && good; })(document.getElementById('username'))

checks.name: Age is a required number from 18 to 99
Age 17 is out of range, 18 is valid
checks.test: (a => { a.value = '17'; const low = a.validity.rangeUnderflow; a.value = '18'; const ok = a.validity.valid; a.value = ''; return low && ok; })(document.getElementById('age'))

checks.name: Website is an optional URL field
Password is required with at least 8 characters
The terms checkbox is required
The form does not disable validation

guide.prereqs: Constraint attributes: `required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and input types. See *Form validation and accessible error handling*.
guide.intuition: The browser can enforce common rules itself if you declare them on the controls. Each rule is one attribute. The input `type` matters too: `min` and `max` only mean something on a number (or date) input, and `type="url"` brings its own format check.
hints: Remove `novalidate` from the form first; while it is present the browser skips every check.

The username needs four attributes: `required`, `minlength`, `maxlength` and a `pattern`. A character class such as `[a-z0-9]+` describes "one or more lowercase letters or digits"; the pattern must match the whole value.
Set `type="number"` with `min`/`max` on age, `type="url"` on website (and nothing else, so it stays optional), `type="password"` with `minlength="8"` on password, and `required` on the checkbox.
guide.approach:
1. Delete `novalidate`.
2. `#username`: `required minlength="3" maxlength="12" pattern="[a-z0-9]+"`.
3. `#age`: `type="number" min="18" max="99" required`.
4. `#website`: `type="url"`.
5. `#password`: `type="password" required minlength="8"`.
6. `#terms`: `required`.
7. Try submitting bad values to see the browser's messages.
guide.pitfalls:
- `pattern` is ignored on an empty value, so it does not replace `required`.
- Writing anchors is unnecessary: the pattern is matched against the entire value automatically.
- `min`/`max` on a text input do nothing.
- Adding `required` to the optional website field.
- Remember that the server must repeat every check; attributes help users, they do not provide security.

web-semantic-skeleton.title: Semantic page skeleton
web-semantic-skeleton.description:
This page is built entirely from `<div>` elements with ids. Replace them with semantic elements. The text can stay as it is.

Requirements:

- `<html>` has a `lang` attribute.
- `<body>` has exactly one `<header>` child and exactly one `<footer>` child, and **no** `<div>` children.
- There is a `<nav>` with a non-empty `aria-label` containing at least three links.
- There is exactly one `<main>`.
- Inside `<main>` there is an `<article>` containing the page's only `<h1>`.
- There is an `<aside>` for the related links.
web-semantic-skeleton.starter:
Tide Times
Home Today This week
Spring tides explained

Twice a month the sun and moon line up and the tidal range is at its greatest.

Related
Neap tides
Data from the harbour office.
web-semantic-skeleton.solution:
Tide Times

Home Today This week

Spring tides explained

Twice a month the sun and moon line up and the tidal range is at its greatest.

Related

Neap tides
Data from the harbour office.

checks.name: html has a lang attribute
body has one header and one footer child
body has no div children
A labelled nav holds at least three links
There is exactly one main
The only h1 is inside an article in main
There is an aside

guide.prereqs: `header`, `nav`, `main`, `article`, `aside`, `footer`, landmarks and the `lang` attribute. See *Semantic page structure*.
guide.intuition: An `id` such as `header` helps you, the author, but tells the browser nothing. The matching element creates a landmark that assistive technology can jump to and that reader modes and search engines can use. Each `div` here already has an obvious role in its name: swap the generic element for the specific one.
hints: Map the ids directly: `#header` to `<header>`, `#nav` to `<nav>`, `#main` to `<main>`, `#footer` to `<footer>`.
The post could be published on its own, so it is an `<article>`; its title is the page's `<h1>`. The sidebar is loosely related content: `<aside>`, with an `<h2>` for its title.
Add `lang="en"` to `<html>` and an `aria-label` such as `Main` to the `<nav>`.
guide.approach:
1. Add `lang` to the root element.
2. Replace the outer three `div`s with `header`, `main`, `footer`.
3. Turn the link group into `<nav aria-label="Main">`.
4. Turn `.post` into `<article>` and its title into `<h1>`.
5. Turn `#sidebar` into `<aside>` and its title into `<h2>`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Confusing `<header>` (a visible region) with `<head>` (metadata).
- Using two `<h1>` elements: the sidebar title is a lower level.
- Writing "Main navigation" as the label: the role already says "navigation", so the screen reader would say it twice.
- More than one `<main>`.

web-details-summary.title: FAQ with details and summary
web-details-summary.description:
Build a three-question FAQ that expands and collapses **without JavaScript**.

Requirements:

- Exactly three `<details>` elements.
- In each one the **first child** is a `<summary>` (the question), followed by at least one more element (the answer).
- The **first** item is open when the page loads; the other two are closed.
- All three have `name="faq"`, so that opening one closes the others.
- The `<summary>` shows a pointer cursor (`cursor: pointer`).
web-details-summary.starter:
Ferry questions

Can I bring a bicycle?

Yes, bicycles travel free on every sailing.

Are dogs allowed?

Dogs are welcome on the outer deck.

Is there a cafe on board?

Hot drinks are served on sailings longer than thirty minutes.
web-details-summary.solution:
Ferry questions

Can I bring a bicycle?

Yes, bicycles travel free on every sailing.

Are dogs allowed?

Dogs are welcome on the outer deck.

Is there a cafe on board?

Hot drinks are served on sailings longer than thirty minutes.

checks.name: There are exactly three details elements
Each details starts with a summary
Each details has answer content after the summary
Only the first item is open
All three share name=faq
The summary has cursor: pointer

guide.prereqs: `<details>`, `<summary>`, the `open` and `name` attributes. See *Semantic page structure*.
guide.intuition: A disclosure widget is built into HTML. `<details>` hides its content until its `<summary>` is activated, works with the keyboard, and reports its expanded state to screen readers. Giving several of them the same `name` turns them into an accordion in which only one can be open.
hints: Replace each `div.item` with `<details>` and each question paragraph with `<summary>`.
The boolean attribute `open` on the first `<details>` makes it start expanded.
Add `name="faq"` to all three, and `summary { cursor: pointer; }` in the CSS.
guide.approach:
1. Convert the three wrappers to `<details name="faq">`.
2. Convert each `.q` paragraph to `<summary>` and keep it as the first child.
3. Add `open` to the first one only.
4. Style the summary with `cursor: pointer` (and anything else you like).
guide.pitfalls:
- Putting the `<summary>` after the answer: it must come first.
- Writing `open="false"` on the others: any `open` attribute means open.
- Hiding the answers with `display: none` yourself: the element already does that.

web-visually-hidden.title: Visually hidden text for an icon button
web-visually-hidden.description:
The button below shows only a magnifying-glass icon, so a screen reader announces "button" and nothing else. Give it a name that is hidden from sight but available to assistive technology.

Requirements:

- Inside the button, add a `<span class="sr-only">` containing the text for the button (for example "Search").
- Write the `.sr-only` class so that the span:
  - is taken out of the layout with `position: absolute`,
  - occupies at most **1px by 1px**,
  - hides its overflow (`overflow: hidden`),
  - does not wrap (`white-space: nowrap`),
  - is **not** hidden with `display: none` (that would hide it from screen readers too).
- The decorative `<svg>` has `aria-hidden="true"`.
web-visually-hidden.starter:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Icon button</title>
<style>
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
button { padding: .5rem; border-radius: 8px; border: 2px solid #37474f; background: white; }
svg { width: 24px; height: 24px; display: block; }
.sr-only {
  /* your code */
}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button type="button">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"><circle cx="10" cy="10" r="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M15 15l6 6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5"/></svg>
</button>
</body>

- The plain `.btn` button keeps `background-color` `rgb(236, 239, 241)` and `color` `rgb(38, 50, 56)`.
- No declaration uses `!important`.
- No selector contains an id (`#`).
- No inline `style` attributes are added.

guide.prereqs: Specificity as three columns (ids, classes, elements) and source order. See *The cascade, specificity and inheritance*.
guide.intuition: `#toolbar .btn` scores (1,1,0). `.btn--primary` scores (0,1,0). The id column is compared first, so the grey rule wins no matter where it appears in the file. Raising the modifier's specificity or adding `!important` would work, but each of those makes the next override harder. The durable fix is to *lower* the selector that is too strong.
hints: Work out the specificity of both selectors that set `background-color` on the Save button.
The base button style does not need to know which toolbar it is in. What is the simplest selector that still matches every button?
Change `#toolbar .btn` to `.btn`. Both rules are now (0,1,0), and the modifier wins because it comes later in the file.

1. Open developer tools on the Save button: the `.btn--primary` declarations are struck through, beaten by `#toolbar .btn`.
2. Replace the selector `#toolbar .btn` with `.btn`.

- Adding `!important` to the modifier: it works today and causes the next conflict tomorrow.
- Writing `#toolbar .btn--primary`: it wins, but ties the button to one container.

- `.required::after` inserts an asterisk `*` coloured `rgb(198, 40, 40)`.

guide.prereqs: Pseudo-elements `::before`, `::after`, `::marker` and the `content` property. See *Introducing CSS*.
guide.intuition: `::before` and `::after` create an extra box inside an element, as its first or last child, without touching the HTML. The box only exists if you give it `content`. That makes them ideal for decoration that should follow a class around: mark a link `external` and the arrow appears.
hints: Every `::before` or `::after` rule needs a `content` declaration, or nothing is generated.
Characters outside the keyboard can be written as a backslash and their code: `content: "\201C"` for the opening quote and `"\2197"` for the arrow.
Colour the asterisk inside the `.required::after` rule itself, and use `li::marker { color: ... }` for the bullets.
guide.approach:
1. `.quote::before { content: "\201C"; }`
2. `a.external::after { content: " \2197"; }` (the leading space separates it from the text).
3. `.required::after { content: " *"; color: rgb(198, 40, 40); }`
4. `li::marker { color: rgb(0, 105, 92); }`

- Forgetting `content`: the pseudo-element does not render.
- Typing the characters into the HTML instead: the decoration would then have to be repeated by hand everywhere.
- Expecting `::marker` to accept any property; it supports only a few, such as `color` and the font properties.
- Putting essential information only in generated content: the `required` attribute on the input is what actually tells assistive technology the field is mandatory.

guide.intuition: `1rem` equals the root font size, which is 16px unless the reader has chosen something else. Sizes written in `rem` therefore scale with that preference, while `px` sizes ignore it. web-button-states.solution:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Button</title>
<style>
body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; display: flex; gap: 1rem; padding: 1rem; }
.btn {
  font: inherit;
  font-weight: 600;
  background-color: rgb(21, 101, 192);
  color: white;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 10px 18px;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: background-color 0.15s ease-out;
}
.btn:hover {
  background-color: rgb(13, 71, 161);
}
.btn:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid rgb(255, 179, 0);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
.btn:disabled {
  opacity: 0.5;
  cursor: not-allowed;
}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<button class="btn" type="button">Book now</button>
<button class="btn" type="button" disabled>Sold out</button>
</body>
</html>

guide.prereqs: Pseudo-classes `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `:disabled`; `outline`; transitions. See *Styling lists, tables and forms* and *Transitions, transforms and animations*.
guide.intuition: A button is a small state machine: resting, pointed at, focused by keyboard, pressed, unavailable. Each state needs its own visual cue so that every kind of user knows what is happening. Hover alone leaves out keyboard and touch users, which is why the focus ring matters as much as the hover colour.
hints: Write the base rule first: colours, `border: 0`, radius, padding, `cursor: pointer`.

Add three more rules: `.btn:hover` (a darker background), `.btn:focus-visible` (an `outline` such as `3px solid` in a contrasting colour, plus `outline-offset`), `.btn:disabled` (`opacity` and `cursor: not-allowed`).
Put `transition: background-color 0.15s;` on the base rule, not on `:hover`, so the change animates in both directions.
guide.approach:
1. Base: `background-color: rgb(21, 101, 192); color: white; border: 0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px 18px; cursor: pointer; transition: background-color .15s;`
2. `.btn:hover { background-color: rgb(13, 71, 161); }`
3. `.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid rgb(255, 179, 0); outline-offset: 2px; }`
4. `.btn:disabled { opacity: .5; cursor: not-allowed; }`
guide.pitfalls:
- `outline: none` with no replacement removes the only indicator keyboard users have.
- Putting `transition` only on `:hover`, so the return snaps.
- A hover rule that also restyles the disabled button; `.btn:hover:not(:disabled)` or ordering the disabled rule last avoids that.
- Signalling the disabled state by colour alone: keep the `disabled` attribute so assistive technology knows too.

- Inside each card there are elements with the classes `product__title`, `product__price` and `product__button`.
- The second card is a sale item: it has **both** `product` and `product--sale`.
- No element in a card has an `id`.
- In the CSS, every selector other than `body` starts with `.product` and contains no id.
- The normal price is `rgb(31, 35, 40)`; the price inside the sale card is `rgb(198, 40, 40)`.

guide.prereqs: BEM naming (`block`, `block__element`, `block--modifier`) and flat specificity. See *CSS architecture: BEM, utilities, modules and layers*.
guide.intuition: The starter's selectors describe *where* things are (`#shop div.box p`), so they break when the markup moves and need `!important` to override. BEM names describe *what* things are. Every part gets one unique class, every selector has the same low specificity, and a variant is a modifier class added next to the block class.
hints: Name the block `product`. Its parts become `product__title`, `product__price` and `product__button`: put those classes on the `h3`, `p` and `button`.
Replace `id="sale-item"` with the modifier: `class="product product--sale"`. Remove the `#shop` wrapper or at least its id.

Rewrite each rule with a single class selector. The sale colour is the one place a two-class selector is normal: `.product--sale .product__price`. It needs no `!important` because (0,2,0) beats (0,1,0).
guide.approach:
1. HTML: add the block, element and modifier classes; delete the ids and the inline style wrapper.
2. CSS: `.product { ... }`, `.product__title { ... }`, `.product__price { ... }`, `.product__button { ... }`.
3. Variant: `.product--sale .product__price { color: rgb(198, 40, 40); }`.
4. Delete `!important`.

- Using the modifier alone (`class="product--sale"`): the card loses all its base styles.
- Nesting element names (`product__body__title`): BEM elements are named after the block only.
- Keeping a tag in the selector (`h3.product__title`), which raises specificity for no benefit.

web-positioned-badge.description:
Pin the red badge to the **top-right corner** of the icon so that it overhangs the corner.

Requirements:

- `.icon` is the reference frame: `position: relative` (it must not move or change size; it stays 48 by 48 pixels).
- `.badge` is `position: absolute`, and its containing block is `.icon`.
- The badge overhangs by **6px**: its right edge is 6px to the right of the icon's right edge, and its top edge is 6px above the icon's top edge.
- The badge is round (`border-radius` of at least 10px, or 50%).

guide.prereqs: `position: relative` and `absolute`, offsets, containing blocks. See *Normal flow, display, positioning and stacking*.
guide.intuition: An absolutely positioned element measures its offsets from the nearest ancestor that is itself positioned. `position: relative` with no offsets leaves the icon exactly where it was but promotes it to that role. Negative offsets then move the badge *outside* the icon's edges.
hints: Parent first: add `position: relative` to `.icon`.
Child next: `position: absolute` on `.badge`, then `top` and `right`.
`right: 0` would line the badge's right edge up with the icon's. To overhang by 6px use `right: -6px`, and likewise `top: -6px`. Finish with `border-radius: 999px`.
guide.approach:
1. `.icon { position: relative; }`
2. `.badge { position: absolute; top: -6px; right: -6px; }`
3. `border-radius: 999px;` makes a pill or circle whatever the number inside.
4. Remove the `position: relative` temporarily to see the badge jump to the corner of the page: that is what a missing reference frame looks like.
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting `position: relative` on the parent.
- Using `left`/`bottom` and trying to calculate the icon's size: `top` and `right` anchor to the corner you care about.
- Positive offsets, which push the badge inward.
- Giving `.icon` offsets as well, which would move it.

web-z-index-stack.description:
Three overlapping cards are drawn in source order, so C (last in the HTML) is on top. Reverse that **with CSS only**, and make sure the toast message stays above everything.

Requirements:

- Do not change the order of the cards in the HTML (A, B, C).
- Card **A** is on top, **B** in the middle, **C** at the bottom: their `z-index` values satisfy A > B > C (all numeric).
- `.stack` forms its own stacking context using `isolation: isolate`, so the cards' z-indexes cannot interfere with the rest of the page.
- `.toast` is `position: fixed` and has a numeric `z-index` of at least 1, which is enough to appear above the isolated stack.
- No `z-index` in the style sheet is larger than **10** (no "9999" arms race).

guide.intuition: `z-index` orders positioned elements, but only against siblings in the same stacking context. `isolation: isolate` turns `.stack` into a sealed group: inside it the cards are ordered 3, 2, 1; from outside, the whole group behaves as one layer at the default level. The fixed toast with `z-index: 1` is therefore above the entire group, even though a card inside has a higher number.
hints: The cards are already `position: absolute`, so `z-index` will take effect on them. Give A the highest value and C the lowest.

Make the toast `position: fixed` and give it `z-index: 1`. Small numbers are enough when contexts are isolated.

1. `.a { z-index: 3; } .b { z-index: 2; } .c { z-index: 1; }`
2. `.stack { isolation: isolate; }`
3. `.toast { position: fixed; z-index: 1; }`
4. Reason it through: the root stacking context contains the stack (level auto) and the toast (level 1); the toast wins. Inside the stack, 3 beats 2 beats 1.
guide.pitfalls:
- Reordering the HTML: that changes reading and tab order too.
- `z-index` on an element with `position: static`: it is ignored.
- Reaching for 9999. Large numbers do not escape a stacking context; they only make the next conflict harder to reason about.
- Forgetting that the toast needs a `position` for both its offsets and its z-index to apply.

guide.intuition: `grid-template-areas` lets you draw the layout as text: each quoted string is a row and each word a column. Repeating a name across a row makes that area span those columns. guide.intuition: The overlay is a fixed box stretched to all four edges of the viewport, so it covers the page and does not scroll. Making that box a grid with `place-items: center` centres its only child, the panel, without any arithmetic. The translucent colour must be an *alpha colour* on the overlay, not `opacity`, because opacity would fade the panel as well. The arithmetic for this frame: the container's content box is 1024 - 32 = 992px. Four columns need 4 x 220 + 3 x 16 = 928px, which fits; five would need 1164px, which does not. - Writing `color: --text` without `var()`.

Naming `transform` and `box-shadow` (instead of `all`) keeps the browser from animating things you did not intend, and `transform` moves the card without disturbing the layout around it.

Requirements:

- An `@keyframes` rule named **`pulse`** with at least two keyframes that change `transform` (or `scale`) and/or `opacity`.
- `.dot` runs `pulse`: its computed `animation-name` is `pulse`, the duration is **1.5s**, the timing function is `ease-in-out`, and it repeats **infinitely**.
- An `@keyframes` rule named **`spin`** that rotates through a full turn.
- `.spinner` runs `spin`: duration **1s**, timing function **`linear`**, repeating **infinitely**.

guide.prereqs: `@keyframes`, the `animation` shorthand and its parts, `transform`. See *Transitions, transforms and animations*.
guide.intuition: An animation has two halves. `@keyframes name { ... }` is the script: a list of snapshots at percentages of the timeline. The `animation` property on an element is the performance: which script, how long, with what easing, how many times. A spinner uses `linear` so its speed never changes and the loop has no visible seam; a pulse uses `ease-in-out` so it swells and settles softly.
hints: Define the scripts first: `@keyframes pulse { ... }` with `from`, `50%` and `to` blocks, and `@keyframes spin { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }`.
Attach them with the shorthand: name, duration, timing function, iteration count.
`.dot { animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite; }` and `.spinner { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }`.
guide.approach:
1. `@keyframes pulse`: scale 1, then about 1.4 at 50%, then back to 1 (optionally with opacity).
2. `@keyframes spin`: only a `to` keyframe rotating 360 degrees; the start is taken from the element's current, unrotated state.
3. Apply each with the `animation` shorthand.
4. In production, wrap decorative motion in a `prefers-reduced-motion` query and give anything that loops for more than five seconds a way to pause.
guide.pitfalls:
- A name in `animation` that does not match the `@keyframes` name exactly (names are case-sensitive): nothing moves.
- Omitting the duration: the default is `0s`, so the animation is invisible.
- `ease` on a spinner: it visibly speeds up and slows down on each turn.
- Animating `width` or `margin` for a pulse: use `transform: scale()` so that no layout work is triggered.
